c.tagline: Colombia's Caribbean 'Golden Gate' — home of the country's biggest Carnival, Shakira, and the reborn Magdalena riverfront.

taxi.fareNote: Barranquilla taxis are unmetered; agree the fare before you set off, or use an app that quotes the price up front.

emergency.note: 123 is Colombia's unified nationwide emergency line for police, fire, and ambulance.

avoid.reason: Caution in southern/peripheral neighborhoods; petty crime downtown

hood_desc: The elegant early-20th-century district of tree-lined avenues, Republican-era mansions, and the landmark Hotel El Prado; the historic heart and the classic place to stay for character.
An upscale, leafy extension of El Prado full of restaurants, rooftop bars, cafes, and boutique hotels; a favorite for dining out and nightlife within walking distance.
A modern, affluent zone of high-rises, malls, and nightlife around the Villa Country and Buenavista shopping areas; convenient and lively with plenty of dining.
The city's business and shopping hub built around the huge Buenavista malls, with international chain hotels; practical, safe, and well-connected but less atmospheric.
A calm, well-to-do residential neighborhood of quiet streets near the golf club and Alto Prado, with a couple of larger hotels; relaxed and secure.

water.note: Officially potable, but most visitors and many locals stick to bottled.

transit.hours: Transmetro trunk buses and feeders run roughly 5:00 AM to 11:00 PM; taxis and ride apps cover late nights.
transit.note: Barranquilla's backbone is the Transmetro bus rapid transit system running on dedicated lanes, supplemented by regular city buses, taxis, and ride apps; there is no metro or tram.
transit.pay: Transmetro is paid with a rechargeable smart card tapped at station turnstiles; regular buses take cash paid to the driver.

bus: Intercity buses to Cartagena, Santa Marta, and Bogotá (Terminal Metropolitano)
train: No passenger rail service (only the Las Flores tourist train to Bocas de Ceniza)

transit.m: Taxi from the airport (in Soledad) to the city center (25-35 min)
Public bus from outside the terminal toward the city (slower, with a walk to the stop)

tip.r: A 10% 'propina voluntaria' is usually suggested or added to restaurant bills; you can accept or decline it.

food.name: Arepa de huevo
food.desc: Corn arepa fried once, split, filled with a whole raw egg and fried again until puffed - the Atlantico breakfast eaten standing up.

places.name: Narcobollo
places.note: Self-service fritos institution open from breakfast; the reference point for coastal frying.

places.name: Cucayo
places.note: Colourful Caribbean kitchen that serves fritos as starters and does a very good arepa de huevo.

places.name: Mercado de Barranquilitas
places.note: Working market where cooks fry arepas to order from dawn for market traders.

food.name: Butifarra soledena
food.desc: Small springy pork-and-beef sausages boiled and sold in bunches with lime and bollo de yuca; a speciality of neighbouring Soledad.

places.name: Butifarras Nando Rojas
places.note: The name locals give when asked who makes the best butifarra on the coast.

places.name: Plaza de Soledad
places.note: Vendors work the church square with baskets of warm butifarra and limes.

places.name: Narcobollo
places.note: Butifarra served with bollo and suero among the fritos counter classics.

food.name: Sancocho de guandu con carne salada
food.desc: Pigeon-pea and coconut soup with salted beef, yam and plantain - Barranquilla's Sunday and Easter pot, thick enough to stand a spoon in.

places.name: Cucayo
places.note: Traditional Caribbean recipes done properly, sancochos included.

places.name: La Cueva
places.note: Restaurant-bar where Gabriel Garcia Marquez and the Barranquilla Group drank; classic coastal menu.

places.name: Palenque Restaurante
places.note: Afro-Caribbean cooking of the region with soups, stews and coconut rice.

food.name: Cayeye
food.desc: Green banana boiled and mashed with garlic and butter, crowned with grated costeno cheese and sour suero - a coastal breakfast plate.

places.name: Narcobollo
places.note: Breakfast counter serving cayeye with cheese, suero and fried egg.

places.name: Cucayo
places.note: Puts regional breakfasts on the menu all day, cayeye among them.

places.name: Palenque Restaurante
places.note: Traditional Magdalena and Atlantico breakfasts with suero atollabuey.

food.name: Fritos costenos
food.desc: The fried repertoire: carimanolas of yuca stuffed with beef, meat empanadas, papa rellena and crisp patacones with cheese.

places.name: Narcobollo
places.note: Trays of carimanolas and empanadas turned out continuously from early morning.

places.name: Picadas y Patacones La Tia Olga
places.note: Known for loaded patacon discs topped with chorizo, cheese and butifarra.

places.name: Mercado de Barranquilitas
places.note: Cheapest and freshest fritos in the city, straight out of the oil.

food.name: Arroz de lisa
food.desc: Rice cooked with smoked mullet and wrapped in bijao leaf, a dish of the fishing villages at the mouth of the Magdalena.

places.name: Cucayo
places.note: Regional rice dishes including lisa done in the traditional leaf wrap.

places.name: Beach kiosks at Puerto Colombia
places.note: Seafront shacks by the old pier serving fried fish, coconut rice and lisa.

places.name: Palenque Restaurante
places.note: Coastal seafood cooking with coconut rice and river fish.

food.name: Jugos naturales de corozo y tamarindo
food.desc: Tropical juices blended to order - tart corozo palm fruit, tamarind, nispero and guanabana - the antidote to Barranquilla heat.

places.name: Mercado de Barranquilitas
places.note: Juice stalls squeeze whatever is in season, including hard-to-find corozo.

places.name: Juice carts on Paseo Bolivar
places.note: Downtown carts pour cold fruit juices and raspao shaved ice all day.

places.name: Cucayo
places.note: Full list of Caribbean fruit juices in water or milk to go with the fritos.

food.name: Cerveza bien fria
food.desc: Ice-cold lager, Aguila above all, brewed in the city and drunk by the small bottle wherever there is a speaker playing salsa.

places.name: La Troja
places.note: Open-air salsa corner and city landmark; cold beer, huge crowd, records spun since 1963.

places.name: La Cueva
places.note: Literary bar turned restaurant, the classic spot for a beer with history on the walls.

places.name: Puerto Colombia malecon
places.note: Waterfront kiosks by the historic pier for sunset beers and fried fish.

landmarks: Gran Malecón del Río
A five-kilometer riverfront promenade along the Magdalena, the city's proudest modern space for strolling, street food, and river breezes.
Ventana al Mundo (Window to the World)
A soaring 45-meter kaleidoscopic monument at the city's gateway, its colored triangles celebrating Barranquilla's spirit as Colombia's Golden Gate.
Casa del Carnaval
The headquarters and museum of Barranquilla's UNESCO-listed Carnival, alive year-round with costumes, cumbia rhythms, and marimonda masks.
Museo del Caribe
An immersive museum celebrating Caribbean Colombia's music, ecology, and storytelling, with a hall devoted to Gabriel García Márquez.
Catedral Metropolitana María Reina
A monumental modernist cathedral of concrete and stained glass, sheltering a massive bronze Christ by sculptor Rodrigo Arenas Betancourt.
Barrio El Prado
A heritage district of palm-lined avenues and eclectic 1920s mansions, considered one of Latin America's finest early garden suburbs.
Bocas de Ceniza
The dramatic point where the Magdalena River meets the Caribbean, reached by a rattling artisanal rail cart along the jetty.
Iglesia de San Nicolás de Tolentino
The neo-Gothic former cathedral on the city's founding plaza, its restored towers anchoring Barranquilla's historic downtown.
Zoológico de Barranquilla
A compact, conservation-minded zoo sheltering jaguars, manatees, and condors, a beloved family institution in the Caribbean city.
Museo Romántico
A quirky history museum inside a former colonial mansion once used as the US consulate, tracing Barranquilla's carnival, its famous visitors and its past.

train.note: No intercity passenger rail - Colombia's network is freight-only. Barranquilla has no metro; the TransMetro bus rapid transit covers the city. Travel between cities is by coach or plane.

intl.to: Maracaibo & Caracas (Venezuela) - via the Paraguachón border, status varies

bus.note: Expreso Brasilia is headquartered here and runs the biggest network on the Caribbean coast, with Cartagena about 2 hours away, Santa Marta 2 and Bogotá 16-18 overnight. The Venezuelan services depend on the border being open - verify before travelling. The terminal is south of the city; book through Pinbus (https://pinbus.com/).

ferry.note: Barranquilla sits on the Magdalena river near its mouth and its port handles cargo, with no scheduled passenger ferry. There are no regular river passenger services on the Magdalena either - the old steamboat routes are long gone.

full.blurb: The walled colonial jewel of the Caribbean coast, about two hours west, with its old town, forts, and beaches.
full.name: Cartagena

full.blurb: Colombia's oldest surviving city about two hours east, the gateway to Tayrona park, Minca, and Caribbean beaches.
full.name: Santa Marta

half.blurb: A historic seaside town just west of the city with a landmark 19th-century pier, breezy beaches, and fresh seafood.
half.name: Puerto Colombia
